newsitem.title: KENYA: Nairobi students clash with police, rallies called.
newsitem.headline: Nairobi students clash with police, rallies called.

text.p: Riot police clashed with stone-throwing Kenyan students in Nairobi on Thursday and an opposition-backed reform alliance called for rallies across the country next week.
Students took to the streets to protest against a proposed government bill calling for students who fail to pay fees to be expelled. They were first addressed by opposition politicians at parliament.
The youths threw stones at cars on the main highway through the capital as their numbers swelled to about 3,000 before they clashed with riot police firing tear gas canisters and rubber bullets.
The students repulsed baton charges and blocked rush-hour traffic for hours, causing chaos in the city centre. Witnesses said about a dozen policemen were injured and several shops looted.
Students also threw tear gas canisters that exploded at police. It was not clear where they had obtained the canisters.

The riots erupted after the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) called nationwide rallies for July 7, a day known in Kiswahili as "Saba Saba" to commemorate a Nairobi rally seven years ago when at least 20 people were killed.
"The NCEC calls upon all Kenyans to commemorate this day by turning up for planned provincial rallies," said NCEC member John Munuve before naming some 50 locations across the country.
The National Convention groups opposition parties, churches, human rights and other bodies. Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi's government has outlawed the rallies and vowed to stop them.
"We shall maintain peace if we are not provoked by the police," said opposition parliamentarian James Orengo, arguing the rallies were not illegal but were "educational meetings".
Munuve said major meetings would be held in the towns of Kisumu and Eldoret in western Kenya, Nakuru, northwest of Nairobi, and in Wajir in the northeast corner of the country.

Opposition activists said they expected trouble on the biggest day of political action so far before the elections later this year. They said the 50 rally locations were chosen to put pressure on security forces, stretching them across Kenya.

The NCEC said that in some places prayers would be held and there was no uniform type of political action to press the Moi government for constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections.
No date for the polls has been set.

Richard Leakey, secretary-general of the Safina opposition party which has not been registered by authorities, said in a statement backing the rallies: "The issue is not whether Mr Moi must go (as president), the demand is for reform."
Leakey, who is also Kenya's former wildlife guardian and a world renowned palaeontologist, said:

"Everyone, everywhere in Kenya should join the Monday action. Stay away from work, close businesses for the day, freeze the country to show Mr Moi and his dwindling supporters the time for dialogue and change has come.
"Safina urges that there be no violence and we hope the security forces and the supporters for reform will not allow themselves to be provoked by thugs and evil people," he added.
Moi has said the opposition planned chaos on Monday and was inciting youths to take part in riots in Nairobi. The president argues there is no time for reforms before polls.
Despite the opposition campaign, Moi, 73, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for five more years because of electoral rules and deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.

The opposition disrupted reading of the budget in parliament on June 19 before a punch-up between politicians. But only a few hundred students challenged a heavy police and paramilitary presence the same day on the semi-deserted streets of Nairobi.
One person died and scores of shops were looted in two days of rioting in Nairobi after security forces broke up a reform rally on May 31 which the government had declared illegal.
